title: UNIT 2: THE NUMBER SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The number system includes natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers and real numbers.

◆ Main sets:
ℕ → Natural numbers
ℤ → Integers
ℚ → Rational numbers
I → Irrational numbers
ℝ → Real numbers

✓ Relationship:
ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ

✓ Both rational and irrational numbers are real numbers:
ℝ = ℚ ∪ I.

title: 2.1 NATURAL NUMBERS AND INTEGERS
notes:
✓ Natural numbers → Positive counting numbers.

ℕ = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}

✓ Integers → Positive numbers, zero and negative numbers.

ℤ = {..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...}

✓ Every natural number is an integer, but not every integer is a natural number.

Example:
3 ∈ ℕ and ℤ
0 ∈ ℤ but 0 ∉ ℕ
−5 ∈ ℤ but −5 ∉ ℕ.

title: EUCLID'S DIVISION LEMMA
notes:
✓ For positive integers a and b, division gives:

a = bq + r

◆ Where:
a → dividend
b → divisor
q → quotient
r → remainder

✓ Condition:
0 ≤ r < b

Example:
128 ÷ 6 gives quotient 21 and remainder 2.

✓ Therefore:
128 = 6(21) + 2.

title: PRIME AND COMPOSITE NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Prime number → A natural number greater than 1 having exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.

Example: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.

✓ Composite number → A natural number greater than 1 having more than two factors.

Example: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.

✓ Important:
1 is neither prime nor composite.
2 is the only even prime number.

title: DIVISIBILITY TESTS
notes:
✓ A number is divisible by:

2 → its last digit is even.
3 → the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
4 → its last two digits are divisible by 4.
5 → its last digit is 0 or 5.
6 → it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
8 → its last three digits are divisible by 8.
9 → the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
10 → its last digit is 0.

Example:
2,334 is divisible by 2 because its last digit is 4.
It is divisible by 3 because 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 12, and 12 is divisible by 3.

title: PRIME FACTORIZATION
notes:
✓ Prime factorization → Expressing a composite number as a product of prime numbers.

Example:
72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3

✓ Therefore:
72 = 2³ × 3².

✓ Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic → Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorization is unique.

Example:
456 = 2³ × 3 × 19.

title: GREATEST COMMON FACTOR (GCF)
LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE (LCM)
notes:
✓ LCM → The smallest positive number that is a multiple of each of the given numbers.

Example:
Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, ...
Multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, ...

✓ Therefore:
LCM(6,15) = 30.

✓ Using prime factorization, take every prime factor with the greatest power appearing in the numbers.

✓ For two positive integers:
GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.

title: 2.2 RATIONAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Rational number → Any number that can be written in the form:

p/q

where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

✓ The set of rational numbers is denoted by ℚ.

ℚ = {p/q : p,q ∈ ℤ and q ≠ 0}

Examples:
3/4, −6, 0, −13/10 are rational.

✓ Every natural number and every integer is rational because:
6 = 6/1
0 = 0/1
−5 = −5/1.

title: TYPES OF FRACTIONS
notes:
◆ Proper fraction → Numerator is smaller than denominator.
Example: 7/8.

◆ Improper fraction → Numerator is greater than or equal to denominator.
Example: 7/3.

◆ Mixed fraction → A whole number together with a proper fraction.
Example: 5 1/4.

✓ Converting mixed to improper:
5 1/4 = (5 × 4 + 1)/4 = 21/4.

title: DECIMAL REPRESENTATION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ A rational number written as a decimal can be:

◆ 1 Terminating decimal → Decimal ends after a finite number of digits.
Example:
3/5 = 0.6

◆ 2 Repeating decimal → A digit or group of digits repeats indefinitely.
Example:
5/9 = 0.555...

✓ Bar notation is used to show repetition:
1/3 = 0.3̅
23/99 = 0.23̅

✓ Every rational number has either a terminating or repeating decimal representation.

title: CONVERTING TERMINATING DECIMALS TO FRACTIONS
notes:
✓ A terminating decimal can be converted to a fraction by using a denominator of 10, 100, 1000, etc.

Example:
7.3 = 73/10.

Example:
−0.18 = −18/100 = −9/50.

◆ Rule:
1 decimal place → denominator 10.
2 decimal places → denominator 100.
3 decimal places → denominator 1000.

title: LOCATING RATIONAL NUMBERS ON THE NUMBER LINE
notes:
✓ Integers can be placed directly on a number line.

✓ Fractions can be converted to decimal form and then located.

Example:
4/3 = 1.3̅
−5/2 = −2.5

✓ Therefore, 4/3 is located between 1 and 2, while −5/2 is located between −3 and −2.

title: 2.3 IRRATIONAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Irrational number → A decimal number that is neither terminating nor repeating.

Examples:
√2, √3, √5, π.

✓ If a is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √a is irrational.

Examples:
√25 = 5 → rational.
√36 = 6 → rational.
√7 → irrational.
√11 → irrational.
√18 → irrational.

✓ 22/7 is rational because it is written as a ratio of integers, even though it is commonly used as an approximation of π.

title: PRINCIPAL SQUARE ROOT
notes:
✓ The radical sign √ is used for square roots.

✓ The principal square root of a positive number is the positive value whose square gives the original number.

Examples:
√4 = 2
√9 = 3
−√9 = −3
√0.0016 = 0.04

✓ For positive a and b:
If a < b, then √a < √b.

Example:
5 < 6, therefore √5 < √6.

title: LOCATING IRRATIONAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Irrational numbers such as √2 can be located on the number line geometrically.

For √2:
1² + 1² = c²
c² = 2
c = √2

✓ Construct a right triangle with both perpendicular sides of length 1. The hypotenuse has length √2. Transfer this length to the number line using a compass.

✓ √2 ≈ 1.4142, so √2 lies between 1 and 2.

title: OPERATIONS ON IRRATIONAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Irrational numbers can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided, but the result is not always irrational.

✓ For positive a and b:
√a × √b = √(ab).

Example:
√2 × √3 = √6.

Example:
(2 + √2)(1 + √5)
= 2 + 2√5 + √2 + √10.

✓ Important:
The product of two irrational numbers can be rational or irrational.

Example:
√2 × √2 = 2 → rational.
√2 × √3 = √6 → irrational.

title: LIKE RADICALS
notes:
✓ Like radicals → Radicals having the same radicand and the same index.

Examples:
2√5 and √5 are like radicals.
2√5/3 and √5 are like radicals.

√2 and √3 are not like radicals.

✓ Only like radicals can be combined directly through addition or subtraction.

Example:
√3 + √12
= √3 + 2√3
= 3√3.

title: SIMPLIFYING RADICAL EXPRESSIONS
notes:
✓ To simplify a radical, factor the radicand into a perfect square and another factor.

Example:
√18 = √(9 × 2)
= 3√2.

Example:
√12 = √(4 × 3)
= 2√3.

Example:
2√18 − √2 + √8
= 6√2 − √2 + 2√2
= 7√2.

title: 2.4 REAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Real numbers → Numbers that are either rational or irrational.

✓ The set of real numbers is denoted by ℝ.

ℝ = ℚ ∪ I

✓ Every point on the number line corresponds to a real number.

◆ Real numbers include:
• Natural numbers
• Integers
• Rational numbers
• Irrational numbers.

Examples:
−4 → rational and real.
3/5 → rational and real.
√2 → irrational and real.
π → irrational and real.

title: COMPARING REAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ For any two real numbers a and b, exactly one of the following is true:

a < b, a = b, or a > b.

✓ This is the trichotomy property.

✓ Transitive property:
If a < b and b < c, then a < c.

✓ For non-negative real numbers:
If a² < b², then a < b.

✓ For positive a and b:
If a < b, then √a < √b.

title: OPERATIONS ON REAL NUMBERS
notes:
✓ Rational numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a non-zero rational number.

✓ Irrational numbers satisfy the commutative, associative and distributive laws for addition and multiplication, but their results are not always irrational.

◆ Important results:
✓ Rational + Irrational = Irrational.
✓ Rational − Irrational = Irrational.
✓ Non-zero Rational × Irrational = Irrational.
✓ Non-zero Rational ÷ Irrational = Irrational.

Example:
5√3 + 2√2 + √2 − 4√3
= √3 + 3√2.

title: 2.4.4 UPPER AND LOWER BOUNDS
notes:
✓ When a number is rounded, its actual value lies within a range.

✓ Lower bound → The smallest possible value before rounding.
✓ Upper bound → The largest boundary value before rounding.

◆ To find bounds:
1. Identify the place value of the stated accuracy.
2. Divide that place value by 2.
3. Subtract this amount for the lower bound.
4. Add this amount for the upper bound.

Example:
872 kg to the nearest kilogram.
Half of 1 kg = 0.5 kg.

✓ Lower bound = 872 − 0.5 = 871.5 kg.
✓ Upper bound = 872 + 0.5 = 872.5 kg.

✓ Therefore:
871.5 ≤ w < 872.5.

title: BOUNDS TO DECIMAL PLACES
notes:
Example:
10.7 correct to 1 decimal place.

Half of 0.1 = 0.05.

✓ Lower bound:
10.7 − 0.05 = 10.65

✓ Upper bound:
10.7 + 0.05 = 10.75

✓ Therefore:
10.65 ≤ x < 10.75.

◆ For a value rounded to the nearest unit, use ±0.5.
◆ For the nearest tenth, use ±0.05.
◆ For the nearest hundredth, use ±0.005.

title: BOUNDS IN CALCULATIONS
notes:
✓ Bounds can be used to determine the possible range of calculated quantities such as sums, differences, products and areas.

Example:
If a length is 10.5 m to the nearest metre, then:
10 ≤ length < 11.

✓ For an area, use the appropriate lower and upper bounds of each dimension and calculate the corresponding minimum and maximum possible values.

title: 2.4.5 SCIENTIFIC NOTATION
notes:
✓ Scientific notation, also called standard notation, writes a number as:

a × 10ⁿ

where:
1 ≤ a < 10
and n is an integer.

✓ Used for very large or very small numbers.

Examples:
1,856,700,000 = 1.8567 × 10⁹
0.000000314 = 3.14 × 10⁻⁷.

title: CONVERTING SCIENTIFIC NOTATION
notes:
✓ To convert an ordinary number to scientific notation:

1. Move the decimal point until exactly one non-zero digit remains before it.
2. Count the number of places moved.
3. Large number → positive exponent.
4. Small number → negative exponent.

Example:
5,370,000 = 5.37 × 10⁶.

Example:
0.00000017 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁷.

✓ To convert back, move the decimal point according to the exponent.

title: UNIT 2 QUICK FORMULA SHEET
notes:
◆ Euclid's division form:
✓ a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b.

◆ Prime factorization:
✓ Composite number = product of prime factors.

◆ GCF × LCM:
✓ GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = ab.

◆ Rational number:
✓ p/q, where p,q ∈ ℤ and q ≠ 0.

◆ Decimal representations:
✓ Terminating decimal → ends.
✓ Repeating decimal → repeats indefinitely.

◆ Irrational decimal:
✓ Neither terminating nor repeating.

◆ Real numbers:
✓ ℝ = ℚ ∪ I.

◆ Radical multiplication:
✓ √a × √b = √ab, for positive a,b.

◆ Bounds:
✓ Lower bound = rounded value − half of place value.
✓ Upper bound = rounded value + half of place value.

◆ Scientific notation:
✓ a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10.
